$comment: Pins the engine template the Windows release export must be built from (restructure item 29, G10).
Two independent jobs, because the failure they guard has two ends:
'patches' pins the SOURCE — the patch files on disk, by sha256, so a silent edit to a patch is
caught before anyone rebuilds a template from it.
'binary_markers' pins the RESULT — byte sequences that must (or must not) appear in the exported
game binary, which is the only check that speaks to what actually shipped.
Verify with tools/verify-engine-template.py; see tools/engine-patches/README.md for the rebuild recipe.
Hash is over the LF form. .gitattributes pins *.patch to eol=lf precisely so this value is
the same on Windows and on the Linux runner — without that rule the file checks out CRLF
under core.autocrlf and this hash fails on whichever platform did not write it.
Applies to the windows-client preset only; the other presets use stock templates by design and
have custom_template/release empty legitimately.
Chosen by MEASURING all three candidates against both real templates rather than by reading the
patch, because two of the three do not discriminate:
GetRawInputBuffer  stock 0  patched 1   <- the only usable marker
GetRawInputData    stock 2  patched 1   <- present in BOTH; the backport REPLACES per-message
calls with the buffered path, so the count falls.
A presence check here passes on a stock build.
RAWINPUTHEADER     stock 0  patched 0   <- a struct type name; compile-time only, never in the
binary. A presence check here fails on a GOOD build.
Both wrong choices are silent in the direction that matters, which is why this list is short.
forbidden is a CONTAMINATION CANARY, and it exists because the required-marker check defeated itself.
Godot's export was baking tools/ into the game pck, and this very lockfile contains the literal string
'GetRawInputBuffer' several times over. So an exported binary contained the marker whether or not the
PATCHED TEMPLATE was used - the count went 1x -> 3x purely from shipped text - and a stock-template
export would have passed the check.
Fixed primarily by excluding dev material (tools/, planning/, tests/, docs/, ci/, .github/) from the
export, which a shipped game pck has no business carrying anyway. This canary is the belt: if anything
ever re-includes this file in a build, the check fails LOUDLY instead of silently becoming a tautology.
Published 2026-07-30 as a PRERELEASE at tag engine-4.6.3-stable-vortex1. Prerelease is load-bearing, not tidiness:
GitHub resolves releases/latest to the newest non-prerelease, and the launcher's primary update feed
is /releases/latest/download/latest.json. A full release here would 404 that manifest and drop every
client onto the unauthenticated API at 60 req/hr, quietly.
ONLY the windows template differs from stock. The patch set touches platform/windows/ exclusively, so
linux and macos carry none of it and are stock-equivalent in behaviour; they are pinned here for
provenance - a template built from known inputs whose hash we can verify - not because they fix
anything. macos is universal (arm64 + x86_64 lipo'd); a single-arch macOS template would refuse to
run on half the Mac fleet, which no marker check can see.
sha256 means THIS EXACT PUBLISHED ARTIFACT, which is what a fetcher needs to verify a download. It is
NOT a reproducibility claim: Godot does not build reproducibly across toolchain versions, so
rebuilding from these same pinned inputs yields a different hash and that must not be read as
tampering. Measured: the first CI windows build and the dev-box build had identical CONFIGURATION and
different bytes. The reproducible pin is patches[] + engine.upstream_tag; binary_markers is what
proves the RESULT carries them.
Every hash below was verified by downloading the published asset and hashing it, not taken from the
API - the value that causes a hard failure should be checked against what a fetcher actually gets.
